499. Swap start allocates a dynamic device; stop targets hardcoded zram0
Batch: 5782 | Execution: 2026-10-01__19-16-34 | Type: resource-object-identity
Task: zram-swap-bash-ubuntu24-5782
Affected command/source nodes: node1
Contract: On `node1`, add at least 512 MB of compressed in-memory swap, active at boot
and preferred over any disk-backed swap.
Properties: 3 Process integrity and lineage, 4 Lifecycle and supervision, 7 Resource safety and control-plane separation, 15 Rerun and automation safety, 17 Change scope and collateral effects
Origin/transition/final context: Agent-generated unit transitions from dynamic allocation to a constant teardown target; final unit inspection and reboot results retained.
Problem: Final zram-swap.service captures dev=$(zramctl --find ...), formats and activates that selected device, but both ExecStop commands hardcode /dev/zram0 and ignore failures. It does not record the allocated device for cleanup.
Observed impact: The unit is active and persists after reboot on the recorded fixture, where the selected device is zram0. A coexistence test with an already allocated zram0 is absent.
Production implication: If zram0 belongs to another workload and this unit receives zram1, stop/restart operates on the wrong swap device and leaves the actual owned device active. Ignoring stop failures obscures the mismatch and reruns can accumulate allocation or lose unrelated swap.
Confidence: High for the recorded behavior; production consequence conditional
Limits: Source-supported ownership mismatch, not an observed wrong-device shutdown. This unit does not establish the same defect in other zram variants; some store and reuse the selected device.

564. Service state and control trust a PID without sufficient process identity
Batch: 8220 | Execution: 2026-10-02__23-55-49 | Type: pid-only-process-control
Task: local-package-repository-bash-ubuntu7-8220
Affected command/source nodes: node1
Contract: On `node1`, serve a package repository from local storage and install a package
from it while the usual remote repositories are unreachable.

Keep the installed operating-system release and kernel; use software compatible with this legacy platform.
Properties: 3 Process integrity and lineage, 4 Lifecycle and supervision, 18 Observability and evidence integrity
Origin/transition/final context: Agent-authored init/PID lifecycle; inspect the actual daemon/helper behavior rather than inferring process lineage from the service name.
Problem: The authored init script bases running/already-running status on a stored PID and kill -0 (or the recorded legacy status -p helper), without checking the expected application, process start identity or ownership of the actual listener.
Observed impact: The nominal service/listener checks succeed. The inspected controls do not exercise PID reuse, a manipulated PID file, listener bind failure after fork or a process that ignores termination.
Production implication: A stale/reused PID can make start skip a missing service and make status report an unrelated process as healthy. PID-based termination can target the wrong process. Where stop discards tracking before confirmed exit, an untracked child can survive and conflict with the next start.
Confidence: High for the recorded behavior; production consequence conditional
Limits: Implementation/control weakness; no actual unrelated process kill, forged PID or observed spoofed listener is claimed. SysV tooling is compatible with these legacy platforms; its use alone is not the finding. SSH supervisor child-cleanup traps exist and were considered, so orphaned tunnel children are not assumed.
